concepts.title: Average and Instantaneous Velocity and Speed
concepts.definition: Average velocity divides the net displacement by the whole time interval, while instantaneous velocity is what a velocity gauge would read at one moment -- the limit of the average as the interval shrinks to zero. Speed is the magnitude side of the story: average speed uses total path length over time, so it can never fall below the size of the average velocity.
concepts.key_idea: Displacement over time gives the average; shrink the interval and you hold the instantaneous value.

concepts.title: Acceleration as Rate of Change of Velocity
concepts.definition: Acceleration measures how quickly velocity changes: the change in velocity divided by the time taken for that change, averaged over an interval or taken instantaneously. Its sign tells whether the object speeds up or slows down along the chosen positive direction.
concepts.key_idea: One velocity change, one time interval -- their ratio is the acceleration, sign included.

concepts.title: Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
concepts.definition: When acceleration stays constant along a straight line, three algebraic relations carry all the motion information: the velocity relation linking v to u, a and t; the displacement relation x = u t + half a t squared; and the time-free link v squared = u squared + 2 a x connecting speeds and displacement directly.
concepts.key_idea: Constant acceleration turns calculus into algebra -- three equations connect the five motion variables two at a time.

concepts.title: Relative Velocity
concepts.definition: The velocity one observer assigns to a moving object depends on the observer's own motion. Relative velocity subtracts the reference object's velocity from the target's: two trains moving the same way differ by the small gap of their speeds, while opposite directions make their speeds add.
concepts.key_idea: Velocity is always measured from somewhere -- subtract the reference velocity to switch viewpoints.

concepts.title: Position, Path Length and Displacement
concepts.definition: Choosing an origin and a positive direction on a straight line lets every position be a signed coordinate. The path length is how far the object actually travelled along its route, while displacement is the straight-line change from start to finish -- equal to path length only when the motion never reverses.
concepts.key_idea: Distance is a scalar tally of the road; displacement is a vector jump from start to end, sign and all.

Final position minus initial position is the displacement; a return to start leaves zero displacement however long the path was.
